Title: Podcast Episode 17: Bridging an Uncertain Time for a Lifesaving Program - The GiveWell Blog

Summary: 
Despite decades of progress, malaria remains a leading cause of death among children under five globally. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC), a highly cost-effective intervention that delivers antimalarial drugs to children under five during peak transmission seasons, has been disrupted by cuts to foreign aid funding. SMC programs, which require precise timing and extensive pre-campaign planning—including training distributors, shipping drugs, and community outreach—were jeopardized in 2025 due to a funding freeze starting in January. GiveWell, which has recommended over $500 million in grants for SMC since 2016 and lists it as a Top Charity, responded by providing funding guarantees for pre-campaign activities in six countries. This action ensured that implementing organizations could proceed with preparations despite uncertainty over U.S. government funding. The effort involved consultations with stakeholders in 10 countries and evaluation of funding needs across 11 countries. Although the process was more time-intensive than typical grants, it strengthened GiveWell’s networks and helped maintain continuity of lifesaving campaigns. According to GiveWell CEO Elie Hassenfeld and Program Officer Natalie Crispin, these guarantees were critical in preventing program collapse. The episode, recorded on November 17, 2025, reflects GiveWell’s ongoing commitment to protecting high-impact public health initiatives amid shifting global funding landscapes.

Title: Podcast Episode 18: Behind the Planet Money ALIMA Grant Story - The GiveWell Blog

Summary: 
This podcast episode from The GiveWell Blog, released on December 9, 2025, follows up on the November 26, 2025, Planet Money episode 'Saving lives with fewer dollars,' which discussed GiveWell's evaluation of a $1.9 million grant to the Alliance for International Medical Action (ALIMA) to sustain primary healthcare, hospital services, and malnutrition treatment in two subdistricts of North Cameroon after unexpected U.S. government aid cuts in January 2025. Title: UNICEF urges media, stakeholders to counter vaccine misinformation

Summary: 
UNICEF has urged media organizations and key stakeholders to lead public health education efforts, particularly in rural areas, to combat the growing spread of misinformation about polio vaccination and other health interventions. Dr Emmanuel Alebiosu, UNICEF Health Specialist, made the appeal during the 'Reporting Polio: Covering Gaps and Milestones' media dialogue in Ilorin, Kwara State, on December 3, 2025. He emphasized the media's role as a credible platform for countering disinformation, especially given the rapid spread of false narratives via social media, while acknowledging the media’s own potential to amplify misinformation. The event also featured Nusirat Elelu, Executive Secretary of the Kwara State Primary Health Care Development Agency, who, through her representative Micheal Oguntoye, outlined the state’s integrated health campaigns set to begin November 29, 2025. These include the Maternal Newborn and Child Health (MNCH) Week and an HPV vaccination drive targeting nine-year-old girls who missed the initial national rollout. The campaigns aim to deliver high-impact, low-cost interventions such as routine immunization, vitamin A supplementation, deworming, nutrition screening, and growth monitoring for children under five. Around 200,000 pregnant women are expected to access antenatal services. Dr Gwomson Dauda from the World Health Organization commended efforts during the October Measles-Rubella campaign and urged stakeholders to apply lessons learned to improve future health initiatives. The WHO defines maternal health as the health of women during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period, with major causes of maternal mortality including haemorrhage, infection, high blood pressure, unsafe abortion, and obstructed labour.

Title: Help Us Respond to an Uncertain Future for Global Health - The GiveWell Blog

Summary: 
In early 2025, the US government cut billions in foreign aid, creating widespread uncertainty in global health and development programs. In response, GiveWell, guided by its principles of cost-effectiveness, rigorous evaluation, and strategic fund allocation, made 98 grants totaling approximately $39 million—just over 10% of its annual funding—targeting urgent, high-impact opportunities. These included funding guarantees for seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) campaigns in Benin, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea, Mali, and Togo, ensuring timely implementation despite funding disruptions. Grants also supported the distribution of 4.4 million insecticide-treated nets in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), procurement of 3 million malaria rapid diagnostic tests for Nigeria, and shipment of three months’ worth of injectable artesunate to Mozambique. Additionally, GiveWell funded technical support units (TSUs) in Burkina Faso, DRC, Malawi, Nigeria, Uganda, and Zambia to help governments prioritize health spending and reallocate resources. Emergency research grants were made to complete durability testing on insecticide-treated nets in Cameroon and Nigeria and to finish the CHoBI7 cholera trial in Bangladesh. To prepare for future challenges, GiveWell strengthened global health data systems by funding state-level child mortality estimates in Nigeria and supporting research on vaccine delivery disruptions in DRC, Madagascar, and Nigeria. Site visits to Malawi provided on-the-ground insights into aid cut impacts. Donors are encouraged to contribute to GiveWell’s All Grants Fund, Top Charities Fund, or Unrestricted Fund to support flexible, evidence-based responses to global health crises.

Title: Indian Supreme Court's order seeks to take bite out of stray dog problem. Observers say it's mostly bark.

Summary: 
The Indian Supreme Court issued a suo motu order on November 7, 2025, directing all states and union territories to remove stray dogs from public spaces such as schools, hospitals, universities, and transport hubs, citing rising dog-bite incidents and threats to human safety, particularly children. The order mandates that dogs taken for preventive medical treatment—such as rabies vaccination—must not be returned to the streets but instead relocated to designated shelters, as India’s 2023 law prohibits culling. However, critics argue the directive is impractical and disconnected from ground realities. Activists and experts, including Dr. Krithika Srinivasan of the University of Edinburgh, point out that rabies cases have declined by 75% between 2003 and 2023, and that the existing Animal Birth Control (ABC) program—based on sterilization, vaccination, and deworming—has been effective in reducing dog populations and rabies transmission. Srinivasan warns that removing dogs without proper infrastructure may trigger a 'perturbation effect,' destabilizing dog populations and increasing bite risks. Ayesha Christina Benn, founder of Neighbourhood Woof, highlights that Delhi alone has about a million stray dogs and only 20 shelters, most of which lack compliance and adequate funding—her NGO receives only $11 per dog for services that cost $16.50. The court’s demand for fencing around institutions within eight weeks is seen as unfeasible. A similar directive issued in August 2025 in the Delhi National Capital Region was rescinded after protests. Akanksha Majumdar, a lawyer and founder of The Philanthropist and the Happy Dog, plans to file a review petition, calling the judgment 'a step in the right direction, but detached from ground reality.' Experts agree that long-term solutions lie in expanding access to post-exposure prophylaxis, ending mass feeding of dogs, and strengthening community-based ABC programs with grassroots support. India recorded 3.7 million dog bites and 54 rabies-related deaths in 2024, with dog population estimates ranging from 9 million (2019 census) to 52 million (2021 survey).

Published date: November 17 2025, 16:50

Title: ECOWAS Commission, MCSG enhance child health through deworming intervention   | Ghana News Agency

Summary: 
The Millennium Child Support Group (MCSG), funded by the Spanish Cooperation through the ECOWAS Commission’s Regional Agency for Agriculture and Food (RAAF), conducted a deworming intervention in Northern Ghana targeting over 420 pupils across Muftul Ulum and Nuriah English and Arabic Schools in Gwollu. This initiative is part of the ongoing School Feeding and Child Nutrition Improvement Initiative and is expected to benefit at least 1,600 schoolchildren across eight basic schools in the Sissala West, Jirapa, Lawra, and Nandom Municipalities. The program aims to reduce malnutrition, prevent parasitic infections, improve cognitive development, and sustain high school attendance and enrolment. The Sissala West District Health Directorate led the deworming exercise alongside community sensitisation sessions for parents and caregivers on nutrition, sanitation, hygiene, and child healthcare. Dr Godfrey Ato Parker, CEO of MCSG, stated the deworming will be conducted every three months from 2024 to 2027, emphasizing that child health is essential for learning performance, retention, and long-term development. Mr Chakurah Dramani, Sissala West District Director of Education, highlighted deworming’s role in enhancing concentration, physical growth, and learning outcomes, noting that combined interventions in feeding, clean water, and deworming strengthen the foundation for quality education. Mr Yakubu Benin, Acting Sissala West District Director of Health Services, urged families to adopt consistent hygiene practices such as handwashing with soap, safe water consumption, and proper toilet use to prevent infections. The deworming activity is a key component of a broader school feeding program designed to increase enrolment, improve attendance, and boost classroom participation. The intervention reinforces the joint mission of the ECOWAS Commission and MCSG to improve child health, nutrition, and educational success across West Africa.

Published date: December 01 2025, 15:01
